tagline: A prophet's argument with God about injustice and the rise of Babylon, answered with the call to live by faith and ending in a song of trust.
overview:
Habakkuk is unusual among the prophets. Most prophetic books carry God's word to the people; Habakkuk records the prophet's questions to God. He begins by asking how long God will tolerate the violence and injustice he sees in Judah. God answers that he is raising up the Chaldeans, the Babylonians, to judge Judah. That answer only deepens the problem: how can a holy God use a nation more wicked than the one it punishes? Habakkuk stations himself on the watchtower to wait for a reply.

God's second answer is the heart of the book. The vision will come at its appointed time; the proud will not stand, but the righteous will live by faith, or faithfulness. A series of five woes then announces that Babylon's greed, violence, and idolatry will destroy it in turn, and it closes with the reminder that the LORD is in his holy temple. The book ends with a prayer-psalm in which Habakkuk recalls God's past deeds, trembles at what is coming, and declares that even if the fig tree does not bud and the fields yield nothing, he will rejoice in the God of his salvation.

Habakkuk matters because it gives voice to a question every believer eventually asks, why God allows evil to continue, and it models a way of asking that is both honest and faithful. Its central line, the righteous will live by faith, became one of the most important Old Testament texts in the New Testament and in the history of the church.
author: The book names its author as Habakkuk the prophet (1:1, 3:1), but gives no father, hometown, or king's reign. Nothing certain is known of him beyond the book. The title prophet, and the musical notes in chapter 3, have led some to suggest he had a role connected with the temple's worship, but this is inference. A later Jewish legend, preserved in the Greek additions to Daniel (Bel and the Dragon), has Habakkuk carry food to Daniel in the lions' den; it is not considered historical. Most scholars treat the book as substantially the work of one prophet, though some think chapter 3, with its separate heading and musical notes, circulated independently before being joined to chapters 1 and 2.
date: The book speaks of the Chaldeans as a power God is about to raise up (1:6), which points to the late seventh century BC, when Babylon was rising. Nabopolassar established the Neo-Babylonian kingdom in 626 BC, Nineveh fell in 612, and Babylon defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605. Many scholars date Habakkuk to the reign of Jehoiakim (about 609 to 598 BC), whose injustice Jeremiah condemns (Jeremiah 22:13-17) and during whose reign Babylon first dominated Judah. Others place it earlier, late in Josiah's reign, before Babylon's power was obvious, since 1:5 says the Babylonian rise would be hard to believe. A few place parts of it after the first deportation of 597 BC.
setting: Habakkuk lived through the collapse of the old order in the Near East. Assyria, which had dominated the region for over a century, fell to a coalition of Babylonians and Medes between 612 and 609 BC. Egypt tried to fill the gap and killed King Josiah at Megiddo in 609 BC, but Egypt was defeated at Carchemish in 605 BC by the Babylonian crown prince Nebuchadnezzar, who became king that same year. Judah became a Babylonian vassal. Inside Judah, the reforms of Josiah gave way under his sons to injustice, violence, and a return to idolatry. Judah rebelled against Babylon, and Jerusalem was captured in 597 BC and destroyed in 587 or 586 BC. Habakkuk wrote as this storm gathered, seeing both Judah's corruption and Babylon's ruthless power.
purpose: Habakkuk was written to help God's people trust him when his ways are baffling. It shows that it is right to bring hard questions to God, that God answers even when the answer is unwelcome, and that he remains just and sovereign over nations he uses and then judges. It calls the faithful to wait for God's appointed time and to live by faithful trust in the meantime. Its closing psalm teaches a kind of joy that does not depend on circumstances, rooted in who God is and what he has done.
story: Habakkuk stands among the Minor Prophets after Nahum and before Zephaniah. Nahum announced the fall of Assyria; Habakkuk addresses the power that replaced it, Babylon. Its questions anticipate the catastrophe that 2 Kings, Jeremiah, and Lamentations record: the fall of Jerusalem and the exile. The book also looks beyond Babylon, as its woes promise that the oppressor will fall and that the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD. Babylon's fall came in 539 BC, when Cyrus of Persia took the city, opening the way for the return from exile. In the Bible's later imagery, Babylon becomes the name for every proud power set against God (Revelation 17 to 18).
christ: The New Testament quotes Habakkuk 2:4 three times. Paul uses it in Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11 to show that righteousness before God comes by faith, not by works of the law, and Hebrews 10:38 uses it to encourage believers to persevere in faith while they wait for Christ's return. The Hebrew word in Habakkuk means faithfulness, steady trust shown in a life, and the New Testament writers use the verse in ways that draw on both faith and faithfulness. Paul also quotes Habakkuk 1:5 in Acts 13:41, warning his hearers not to scoff at the work God is doing in their days, the resurrection of Jesus. More broadly, the book's question of how a holy God can deal with evil without either ignoring it or destroying everyone finds its answer, in Christian confession, at the cross, where God judges sin and justifies those who trust him.
reading: Habakkuk is a dialogue followed by a psalm. Read chapters 1 and 2 as a conversation, noticing who is speaking (the prophet complains in 1:2-4 and 1:12-2:1; God answers in 1:5-11 and 2:2-20). Chapter 3 is a prayer set to music, with Selah markings and a note for the choirmaster, and it describes God's coming in the language of storm and warfare drawn from Israel's memory of the exodus and Sinai. A common misreading takes the book as simple doubt answered by a rebuke; in fact God never rebukes Habakkuk for asking. Another misreading takes 2:4 as though it were only about intellectual belief; in its setting it is about steady, trusting loyalty to God through a coming disaster.

structure.title: First complaint: how long will injustice go on?
structure.summary: Habakkuk cries out about violence and the paralysis of justice in Judah.

structure.title: God's answer: the Chaldeans are coming
structure.summary: God announces that he is raising up the ruthless Babylonians to judge Judah.

structure.title: Second complaint: why use the wicked?
structure.summary: Habakkuk asks how a pure God can let a more wicked nation swallow the more righteous, then waits on his watchtower.

structure.title: God's answer: the vision, faith, and five woes
structure.summary: God commands that the vision be written down, declares that the righteous will live by faith, and announces five woes on Babylon's greed, violence, exploitation, and idolatry.

structure.title: Habakkuk's prayer
structure.summary: A psalm recalling God's mighty coming, ending with the resolve to rejoice in God even when everything fails.

themes.title: Honest lament
themes.body: Habakkuk's opening words, how long, belong to the language of the lament psalms. The book shows that faith can argue with God, bring its confusion into the open, and still be faith. God answers the prophet's questions rather than silencing them.

themes.title: God's sovereignty over the nations
themes.body: God raises up Babylon to judge Judah and then judges Babylon for its own pride and violence. Nations act freely and are responsible for their actions, yet they cannot move outside God's purposes. The book holds these truths together without fully explaining how.

themes.title: Living by faith
themes.body: The central answer of the book is not an explanation but a way to live: the righteous will live by faith. Faithfulness means trusting God's word and remaining loyal to him while the vision waits for its appointed time. This line became central to the New Testament and to the Reformation.

themes.title: The self-destruction of greed and violence
themes.body: The five woes of chapter 2 show evil undoing itself. The plunderer is plundered, the house built by violence cries out against its builder, and the idol maker trusts a lifeless thing. God's judgment often works through the consequences of sin itself.

themes.title: Joy without circumstances
themes.body: The book ends not with the problem solved but with a prophet who can rejoice in God though the crops and flocks fail. His joy rests on God's character and past faithfulness, not on present evidence.

keyChapters.why: The two complaints and God's unsettling answer frame one of the Bible's most honest wrestlings with the problem of evil.
The command to wait for the vision, the declaration that the righteous will live by faith, and the five woes form the book's theological center.
The closing prayer, with its vision of God's coming and its resolve to rejoice in God though everything fails, is one of the great confessions of trust in Scripture.
